The earlier sections built models and scored them on new sites. A score says how well a
model predicts, not what it learned. This section reads a fitted model and its
predictions, on the same simulated survey as the rest of the course, and ends with the
report that goes with it.
The first three pages read a random forest from outside, by changing its inputs and
watching its predictions:

- **feature importance**: shuffling one input on the test sites shows how much the
  forest relies on it, and inputs that carry the same information share the credit;
- **partial effects**: a partial dependence plot draws how the prediction changes along
  one input, and ICE curves draw it station by station; the temperature hump appears at
  nearly every station;
- **explaining one prediction**: SHAP values split a single station's prediction into a
  contribution from each input, starting from the average prediction.

The next one reads a model from its parts:

- **interpretable models and surrogates**: a GAM's curves read as a habitat
  description, and a small tree fitted to the forest's predictions copies its broad
  shape, as far as its fidelity goes.

The last one turns the analysis into a report:

- **reporting a model**: the raw data, the code, the seeds and the software versions
  let anyone re-run the analysis, and a model card, written from the code, says what the
  model is for, how well it predicts and where it holds.

The section picks up threads from earlier ones.
[Random forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) built
the forest that the first three pages read.
[Linearity and nonlinearity](../06-assumptions-limitations/linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd)
drew the forest's temperature hump, and [Partial effects](partial-effects.qmd) draws it
station by station.
[Interpretable models and surrogates](interpretable-models.qmd) reads the GAM's parts
with the multipliers of
[Regression for counts](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd), and judges a
surrogate with the R² of
[Information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd).
[Uneven sampling and extrapolation](../06-assumptions-limitations/sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd)
showed where a model's data run out, and [Reporting a model](reporting-a-model.qmd)
writes that range into the model card.

## Further resources

**Documentation**

- [Explaining models and predictions](https://www.tmwr.org/explain.html), Tidy Modeling with R. Local and global explanations through `DALEX`, in tidymodels idiom.
- [DALEX](https://modeloriented.github.io/DALEX/), Przemyslaw Biecek and others. Model-agnostic explanation for R and Python both.
- [Permutation importance](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/permutation_importance.html) and [partial dependence and ICE](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/partial_dependence.html), scikit-learn user guide. The permutation page shows what inputs that move together do to the scores.
- [SHAP](https://shap.readthedocs.io/), Scott Lundberg and others. The Python package for SHAP values, with worked examples for many kinds of model.
- [Interpretable Machine Learning](https://christophm.github.io/interpretable-ml-book/), Christoph Molnar. A free book, and the standard reference for every method named here.
- [Model Cards for Model Reporting](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993), Margaret Mitchell and others (2019). The paper that proposed the model card.
